paras: The killing of Columbus Hill was the fatal stabbing of a Black bootblack by Daniel Sullivan, a white man, opposite the Hanover Market in South Baltimore, Maryland, on the night of August 20, 1881. Police arrested Sullivan within minutes while a large Black crowd followed them threatening to lynch him, and a wire report of an "apparently unprovoked and wanton" killing ran from New York to Minnesota.

The stabbing came a week after another killing a few yards away, in which, the Chicago Tribune noted, a Black man was the killer. Hill, about 25, was a bootblack and handyman known at the Maltby House, while Sullivan, 30, was called a "notorious character" with repeated arrests for larceny.

In the version carried by the Chicago Tribune and the Baltimore German daily Der Deutsche Correspondent, Hill brushed against Sullivan on the crowded Camden Street sidewalk, said "Beg pardon, boss, I didn't mean it," and was stabbed in the chest. Sullivan threw the knife into the street and ran, and the wire report said the act was done almost in the presence of a policeman. A police wagon took Hill to the Southern District station, where he died.

Sullivan was caught within ten or fifteen minutes, by officer Grossmann according to the Correspondent. The cry of murder had drawn nearly a thousand Black people, and the Tribune said the officers had to wait for reinforcements, "so excited was the crowd that followed them threatening revenge and lynching." The Correspondent wrote that the crowd made as if to take Sullivan out of the station and lynch him until Captain Delanty locked one man in a cell, after which it dispersed.

An autopsy the next morning found a wound between the fifth and sixth ribs reaching the heart, and Hill was buried in the city cemetery. At Coroner Bell's inquest that evening, witnesses said Hill had cried out that "Danny" Sullivan did it, and Perry Tolson, a Black neighbor, testified that Sullivan begged him not to betray him. The jury found that "Dennis Sullivan" had stabbed Hill in the heart, and Sullivan was committed to jail to await the grand jury. No report of an indictment or trial was found in coverage through September.

The Chicago Tribune's special dispatch, headed "Cold-Blooded Murder," called Sullivan "the white villain" and Hill "an inoffensive colored man." It framed the case in racial terms: "This time a white man was the murderer and an inoffensive colored man the victim, while last week it was just the opposite." It also wrote that the Black crowd gave chase on learning that "one of their color had been murdered in cold blood by a white man."

The shorter wire report ran on August 22 in the Washington Evening Star and National Republican, the New-York Tribune and the St. Paul Daily Globe, and later in Maryland weeklies. Headlines followed its "unprovoked and wanton" line: "A Brutal Baltimore Murder," "Murdered Without Cause," "Murder of a Bootblack." These versions did not give Sullivan's race, and one-line items under "Tragical Tales" cut the story further, one naming the killer "David Sullivan."

Der Deutsche Correspondent covered the case at length under "Mord nahe dem Hanover-Markte," praising the prompt arrest and printing the inquest testimony. It portrayed the Black crowd as noisy and said Delanty jailed one man to cool his thirst for blood and hanging.

Inquest witnesses described the encounter differently: Rosa Walter testified that Hill bumped a man's arm and apologized and the man refused and struck him. Johann Friedrich, a market stallholder, said instead that Sullivan told Hill to go away with a racial slur and tried to hit him, and that Hill stepped back swinging his blacking box and warned him off before he was stabbed.

The hour ranged from "near midnight" in the Tribune to between 10 and 11 in the inquest verdict. Hill died almost at once on the pavement according to the Tribune, at the station within minutes according to the wire report, and an hour later according to the Westminster Democratic Advocate.

bases: A single white assailant fatally stabbed a Black man in a street encounter (A3, A5); no white crowd took part, and the only crowd was a Black one that threatened to lynch the assailant (A3, A5), so neither mob_assault nor lynching fits.

A Chicago Tribune special dispatch (A3), the Associated wire report (A2, A4) and the local Baltimore German daily with inquest testimony (A5) independently agree that Sullivan stabbed Hill to death near the Hanover Market on August 20 and was arrested.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune special dispatch
accounts.gist: Hill brushed against Sullivan in the crowd, apologized ('Beg pardon, boss'), and was stabbed in the breast without further provocation; a Black crowd of nearly a thousand pursued with the police, threatening lynching.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Hill was stabbed in an apparently unprovoked and wanton act almost in the presence of a policeman, died at a police station, and Sullivan, a notorious character, was promptly arrested.

accounts.label: Inquest witness Rosa Walter
accounts.gist: Hill bumped a passing man's arm and apologized; the man refused the apology and struck him, then threw something under a wagon and ran.

accounts.label: Inquest witness Johann Friedrich
accounts.gist: Sullivan, lifting a drunken man from the sidewalk, told the approaching Hill to go away with a slur and tried to hit him; Hill stepped back swinging his blacking box and warned him not to hit him, and Sullivan stabbed him.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Hill died of a stab to the heart inflicted by Dennis Sullivan on the evening of August 20 between 10 and 11 on Camden Street between Hanover and Sharp.

framing.detail: Chicago Tribune headline 'Cold-Blooded Murder'; calls Sullivan 'the white villain' and Hill 'an inoffensive colored man', contrasting it racially with the previous week's killing.
Wire item calling the act 'apparently unprovoked and wanton', under headlines 'A Brutal Baltimore Murder', 'Murdered Without Cause', 'Murder of a Bootblack'.
Der Deutsche Correspondent calls Sullivan 'der Mörder' and a notorious character, praises the prompt arrest, and describes the Black crowd at the station as noisy and thirsting for blood and hanging.
